key_concepts.concept: Badminton footwork is a repeating movement cycle, not isolated steps.
key_concepts.details: A rally movement should be modeled as cue-read, split-step, first push, travel pattern, stroke-position landing or lunge, recovery, and re-split for the next opponent contact.

key_concepts.concept: The split-step creates readiness only when it is timed to the opponent's strike.
key_concepts.details: A useful split-step lands as the opponent's shot information becomes available, widens the base, flexes hips/knees/ankles, and lets the player push immediately in the chosen direction.

key_concepts.concept: Court speed usually fails at the first push, not at top speed.
key_concepts.details: The first step should be a directional push from a balanced base, with the trunk inside the support base and racket-side/non-racket-side lead chosen by the target area and recovery need.

key_concepts.concept: Base is not a fixed dot; it is the best recovery position for the opponent's likely replies.
key_concepts.details: A player recovers toward a base that reflects own shot quality, opponent position, straight-versus-cross options, format, handedness, and whether the next threat is front, mid, or rear court.

key_concepts.concept: Six-corner coverage is solved by matching footwork pattern to distance, direction, and time.
key_concepts.details: Forecourt corners often require split-step, chasse or running step, lunge, and chasse recovery. Midcourt sides bias fast lateral chasse or block-step recovery. Rear corners require running/cross steps, hop/pivot, scissor kick, jump, and forward recovery.

key_concepts.concept: The movement after contact is part of the skill.
key_concepts.details: Players who arrive well but recover tall, crossed, or late still lose coverage. Recovery should preserve posture, racket readiness, and enough time to split-step again.

key_concepts.concept: Singles rewards whole-court balance; doubles rewards shared coverage and interception.
key_concepts.details: Singles players must cover all six areas alone and bias base by likely reply. Doubles players cover narrower zones, switch between front/back attack and side-by-side defense, and coordinate rotation so neither partner duplicates the same lane.

key_concepts.concept: Fatigue errors often appear as stiffer, taller, later movement before obvious slowing.
key_concepts.details: Under fatigue, players may split late, land stiff, reduce knee flexion, overstride into lunges, recover upright, cross feet at bad times, and abandon base-position discipline.

key_concepts.concept: Not all footwork volume stresses the body the same way.
key_concepts.details: Forward lunges, backhand-side lunges, rear-court jump landings, repeated chasse steps, and scissor-kick recoveries create different lower-limb, trunk, and tendon demands.

key_concepts.concept: Shadow patterns build mechanics, but court coverage must become perceptual and reactive.
key_concepts.details: Teach clean patterns first, then add shuttle feed, directional uncertainty, opponent cue reading, scoring constraints, fatigue, and format-specific movement decisions.

technical_models.model: Opponent contact cue -> split-step landing -> first directional push -> travel pattern -> stroke-position action -> braking/landing -> recovery toward base -> re-split.

technical_models.movement: A shallow rebound from a ready stance that lands just as opponent shot direction becomes readable.
Explosive first push out of split-step using the outside/opposite leg to project the body toward the shuttle.
A quick side-travel pattern where one foot leads and the other foot follows without the feet crossing.
A distance-covering step in which the trail leg crosses in front or behind to help travel toward rear-court or wide-court positions while preserving orientation.
A braking and reaching action, usually into forecourt or wide midcourt, with the lead foot/knee aligned toward the shuttle and the body controlled over the base.
A rear-court jump/rotation pattern in which the legs switch in the air to convert backward movement into forward recovery.
Any airborne stroke-position action should land with enough hip/knee/ankle flexion and trunk control to absorb force and recover into the next split-step.
The return movement after contact toward the highest-value ready position for the next shot.

technical_models.coverage_logic: One player covers all six areas and must balance attacking position with protection against the largest open space.
Two players share court coverage through attacking front/back shape, defending side-by-side shape, and rotation when the attack or defense changes.

tactical_rules.rule: Split-step timing should be anchored to the opponent's strike, not to the player's own previous shot.
Recover toward the position that covers the opponent's most likely high-value replies; do not always recover to geometric center.
Every movement pattern must include braking and recovery; getting to the shuttle without a recovery solution is incomplete footwork.
Use chasse for controlled short-to-medium lateral movement and cross steps when distance or rear-court travel demands it.
Increase lunge speed and range only while lead foot, knee, hip, and trunk alignment remain controlled.
Rear-court jump and scissor-kick actions should help the player rotate and recover forward rather than landing backward and static.
In singles, base position after contact should shift with the quality, direction, and likely reply created by the player's own shot context.
In doubles, movement recovery should rebuild the pair's shape: front/back when attacking, side-by-side when defending, and rotational coverage during transitions.
When fatigue causes late splits, stiff landings, knee collapse, or repeated overstriding, reduce complexity before adding more court volume.
Shadow movement should progress to feeds, random directions, opponent cues, and scoring constraints once the base pattern is technically stable.

physical_demands.quality: Repeated short acceleration, braking, and re-acceleration over one to four steps.
physical_demands.training_notes: Use short-court starts, six-corner feeds, and rally simulations with technical-quality gates.

physical_demands.quality: Hip, knee, ankle, calf, and foot capacity to absorb a lunge and push back to base.
physical_demands.training_notes: Build controlled lunge range, split stance strength, deceleration, and reactive recovery before heavy repeated multi-shuttle lunges.

physical_demands.quality: Rapid stretch-shortening ability for split-step rebound, chasse contacts, jump takeoff, and quick recovery steps.
physical_demands.training_notes: Progress pogo, skipping, low-level hops, lateral bounds, and badminton-specific rebound drills by landing quality.

physical_demands.quality: Balance and frontal/transverse-plane control during lunges, side stops, and one-leg recoveries.
physical_demands.training_notes: Use single-leg holds, hop-stick drills, lateral deceleration, and unstable recovery positions only after baseline alignment is clean.

physical_demands.quality: Hip abductor, adductor, and external-rotator control to keep knees aligned and recover from wide lunges.
physical_demands.training_notes: Include lateral strength, Copenhagen-style progressions when appropriate, split squat variations, and controlled lateral bounds.

physical_demands.quality: Trunk and hip rotation control for scissor-kick, rear-court turns, and safe landing orientation.
physical_demands.training_notes: Pair thoracic/hip rotation mobility with medicine-ball patterns, rear-court shadow movement, and landing orientation coaching.

physical_demands.quality: Aerobic capacity supports repeated high-intensity efforts and recovery between rallies, games, and sessions.
physical_demands.training_notes: Condition with badminton-specific intervals plus enough general aerobic work to maintain movement quality late in sessions.

physical_demands.quality: Reading opponent cues and selecting the correct movement pattern under uncertainty.
physical_demands.training_notes: Move from coach signal to shuttle feed to opponent-fed and live-rally constraints.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: High-volume or high-speed lunges with foot/knee mismatch can increase knee, ankle, and plantar load stress.
Fatigue can reduce knee flexion and increase leg stiffness, raising lower-limb load during lunges and landings.
Rear-court jumps, scissor-kick landings, and repeated rebounds can overload calf and Achilles tissues, especially in recreational players or after load spikes.
Backhand-side and wide lunges can expose the ankle to inversion or poorly controlled edge loading when the player is late or fatigued.
Repeated split-step, jump, lunge, and deceleration work can irritate the patellar tendon or anterior knee if load rises faster than tissue capacity.
Repeated hard-court starts, stops, and lunges can overload foot, shin, and plantar tissues.
Late rear-court turns, poor scissor-kick rotation, and repeated cross steps can increase low-back or hip stress when rotation is forced through the spine instead of shared by hips and trunk.
Doubles players can collide or leave lanes exposed when both recover to the same space or rotate without a clear trigger.

training_implications.summary: Start with ready posture, safe spacing, low center of gravity, split-step on signal, simple chasse, lunge alignment, and recovery to a visible base marker.
Build full-court patterns and recovery: forecourt lunge, midcourt lateral coverage, rear-court cross step, hop/pivot, scissor-kick landing, and base adjustment.
Move from pattern execution to opponent-cue reading, deceptive base shifts, format-specific court coverage, repeated high-intensity rally movement, and fatigue-resistant technique.
Track footwork load by movement type rather than court minutes only.
training_implications.planning_rule: Increase one high-load channel at a time, and use 24-hour ankle, knee, Achilles, shin, hip, and back response to decide whether to progress.

training_implications.summary: Movement conditioning should stop, slow, or simplify when technical errors become repeated.
Preplanned footwork teaches mechanics; reactive footwork teaches badminton coverage.
Singles movement blocks should emphasize whole-court recovery and base bias; doubles blocks should emphasize partner spacing, front/back attack, side-by-side defense, and transition triggers.
Assessment should include technical quality, coverage decision, and load response.

backend_records_to_create.summary: Deep badminton footwork and court coverage section covering movement cycle, split-step, first step, chasse, cross step, lunge, scissor kick, landing, recovery, six-corner coverage, singles/doubles differences, fatigue errors, load risk, and teaching progression.
Opponent contact cue, split-step, first push, travel pattern, stroke-position action, braking/landing, recovery, and re-split should be treated as one repeatable movement cycle.
Split-step should land as opponent shot information becomes available; big early jumps and late flat-footed reactions should be corrected before speed is progressed.
First step should push directionally from a balanced split; chasse is preferred for controlled short-to-medium lateral coverage and recovery, while cross steps cover larger distances.
Lunges should align lead foot, knee, and contact direction, absorb through hip/knee/ankle flexion, and include an immediate push-back recovery.
Rear-court scissor-kick and jump landings should use trunk/hip rotation, useful foot orientation, quiet force absorption, and forward recovery to reduce static or backward landings.
Map forehand/backhand forecourt, forehand/backhand midcourt, and forehand/backhand rearcourt to preferred movement patterns, recovery routes, and load risks.
Singles movement should bias whole-court base recovery; doubles movement should rebuild pair shape through front/back attack, side-by-side defense, and clear rotation triggers.
Track movement load by split-step rebounds, lunges, wide lunges, rear-court jumps, scissor kicks, cross steps, multi-shuttle reps, and live rally minutes rather than total practice time only.
Regress or stop high-speed footwork when late splits, stiff landings, knee collapse, ankle instability, failed recovery, or doubles overlap repeats.
Ready posture and balance games -> signal split-step -> chasse -> static lunge -> split-step/chasse/lunge -> recovery to marked base.
Link forecourt, midcourt, and rear-court movement patterns into six-corner shadowing, fed shuttles, scissor-kick recovery, and base adjustment.
Train opponent-cue split-step, random six-corner feeds, tactical base bias, singles/doubles movement scenarios, and fatigue-resistant landing quality.
Assess whether the player lands split-step on time, pushes in the correct direction without false steps, and reaches the shuttle without losing posture.
Assess lead foot/knee alignment, force absorption, push-back recovery, scissor-kick landing, and ability to re-split before the next feed.
Assess six-corner movement quality, pattern choice, base recovery, and decision-making under both preplanned and random feed conditions.
Assess whether a pair restores front/back attack, side-by-side defense, and rotation coverage without lane overlap or collision risk.
